newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strikes hit French rail, air, sea traffic.
newsitem.headline: Strikes hit French rail, air, sea traffic.

text.p: Strikes disrupted French air, sea and rail traffic on Friday, halting many trains, cutting half the flights at airlines Air France Europe, TAT and Air Liberte and stranding ferries to Corsica and Tunisia.
Train conductors who had been due to end a 36-hour strike over wages and working conditions at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) extended their protest in various regions.
Trains cannnot leave without conductors who are responsible for safety, and the state railway company SNCF said traffic was heavily disrupted, with the south of the country worst hit.
One third of high-speed trains were running between Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Toulouse. Two thirds ran to Bordeaux. Regional trains were cut by one third to two thirds.
Eurostar trains between Paris and London and high-speed links to Brussels were unaffected.

Six trade unions called the strike over wages and working conditions, a new sign of labour unrest and opposition to the government's austerity measures to comply with budget criteria to join the single European currency.
Austerity and the euro are major issues in the current campaign for early elections set for May 25 and June 1.
Air France Europe cut flights by 55 percent on Friday as pilots began a two-day strike over reforms of their pay and working conditions in a merger with parent company Air France.
An airline spokesman said he expected similar disruption on Saturday.

Air Liberte and TAT, French units of British Airways, again cancelled almost half of their flights due to a two-week-old strike by pilots and cabin crew who say a merger of the two airlines will affect their pay and conditions.
A spokesman for the two airlines said they had cancelled 40 percent of flights on Friday and would cancel 30 percent on Saturday and 40 percent on Sunday.
A strike against planned job cuts at Societe Nationale Corse-Mediterranee stranded ferries between Corsica and the mainland French ports of Nice and Marseille, and halting a crossing from Tunis.
